newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE expects $3 bln from offset scheme investments.
newsitem.headline: UAE expects $3 bln from offset scheme investments.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates expects Western companies it buys weapons from to invest in projects which would inject $3 billion into its oil-driven economy over the next seven years, an official said on Tuesday.

The investments would be made under the UAE's offset scheme which requires international defence contractors seeking big contracts to invest part of the value of the deal in profitable joint ventures with local investors.

The UAE Offsets Group (UOG) was launched in July 1990 when Abu Dhabi began a shopping spree for advanced weaponry that has lured a procession of international arms makers seeking multi-billion dollar deals.
"The obligations that we have left over are about $3 billion but we anticipate that will increase," UOG chairman Amin Badr el-Din told Reuters.
"There will be three to four major projects and dozens of smaller projects over the next seven years and probably one or two big ones this year," he added.
Some arms makers say they are frustrated by a lack of investment opportunities in the oil-lubricated economy, which has only a small industrial base.
Badr el-Din reiterated that the UOG had no intention of relaxing its requirements, which military companies say are too stringent.
"There are clearly some structural problems in the economy," he said when asked about complaints by Western companies.
"There was a reluctance in the private sector to invest in capital equipment. People thought it was risky to put money in industry because of the trading tradition here," he added.

Nineteen projects ranging from a shipbuilding company to a medical diagnostic centre have been launched. Badr el-Din said that so far, offset projects had channelled 1.8 billion dirhams ($490 million) into the UAE's economy.
Abu Dhabi has emerged as a key customer in the international arms bazaar, luring major Western weapons makers eager to cash in on the emirate's appetite for high-tech military hardware.
But some companies say they are frustrated by the task of investing in unfamiliar, non-military ventures.

One major complaint is that defence companies are required to invest in projects with local investors in 49/51 percent joint ventures that generate added value to the UAE over a period of seven years equivalent to 60 percent of the value of the sales contract.

Badr el-Din said Western arms makers engaged in the offset scheme were hoping to take over services provided by the government and were increasingly eyeing investment opportunities in the financial sector.
"There is an increasing trend to invest in financial services and a number of projects coming through that are financial in nature," he said.
He said the offset programme could gain momentum because companies were now focusing on launching larger projects, which could eventually be publicly floated.
